title: I have sinned (2 Samuel 12:13)
hookLine: David answers in two Hebrew words, with no excuse
last: THE JUDGE HAS WRITTEN HIS OWN VERDICT.

lines: A KING COULD SAY MANY THINGS.
cards: Nathan has just finished speaking. The room is quiet. A king who has had a man killed now stands accused, in his own palace, by someone with no army behind him.
There are plenty of things a king could say next. He could call the guards. He could explain the pressures of war, or point out that Uriah died in battle, which, on paper, is true.
He could ask who else knows. The text gives him none of those lines. It gives him one short answer.

teach.h: TWO WORDS IN HEBREW. NO BECAUSE.
teach.b: Here it is: "I have sinned against the LORD." In Hebrew it's two words, chatati l'Adonai. No because.
No but. Hear it next to another king. In the first book of Samuel, Saul is confronted by the prophet Samuel after he disobeys a command.
Saul also says I have sinned, and then keeps going: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice. The reason does some of the work of an excuse. David's sentence stops where it starts.
Nathan's reply comes just as fast: the Lord has put away your sin; you shall not die. That doesn't mean nothing follows.

The next words say the child born to David will die, and the chapters ahead are full of trouble in his house. Forgiveness here is real, and so are the consequences, and the text doesn't flatten either.

Jewish tradition calls this kind of turning teshuvah, returning. The heading of Psalm fifty-one ties that psalm to this moment, when Nathan came to David, and some readers hear it as the long version of these two words.
What makes the short answer matter isn't that David feels bad. A person can feel bad and still explain. He stops defending himself.
He names what he did and lets it stand.

teach.h: I HAVE SINNED AGAINST THE LORD.
teach.b: He wronged Uriah, and Bathsheba, and the people he commanded, yet he says, against the Lord.
Some hear that as the deepest admission: every wrong to a person is also a wrong before God.
The sentence is short. It is not small.

how: Jews speak of teshuvah, returning, as naming a wrong, regretting it, and changing course; David's answer to Nathan can be read alongside Psalm 51, which its heading links to this moment.

o: I am forgiven, the prophet's word to David
a sin offering brought to the altar
I have sinned, said with no excuse after it

games.q: I have sinned — tap the pairs.
p: I have sinned against the Lord
I have sinned, because I feared the people
the Lord has put away your sin
its heading points to this moment

s: David gave Nathan a long explanation
he answered with one short sentence: I have sinned against the Lord.
forgiveness meant nothing else would follow
Nathan says David shall not die, and in the next breath says the child will.
Saul also once said I have sinned
and then added a reason: because I feared the people.

games.q: you're David. a prophet has just told you, in your own palace, that you are the man. what do you say?
o: I have sinned against the Lord.
games.why: David says it plainly, with no reason attached, and Nathan answers at once that his sin is put away.

practice: Let one recent thing come to mind where you got it wrong, a sharp word, a broken promise, a corner cut, and say it to yourself in one plain sentence: I did this.
Notice the urge to add because, and let the because go, so the sentence stands on its own. If you pray, you can bring it before God the same way.
